title: One request through a platform
summary: A developer asks for a new service and the platform answers in one flow.

steps.n: The developer picks a template in the portal and answers three questions: name, owner and language.
The portal passes the answers to a workflow that will create everything in order.
The workflow checks the name is free, the owner team exists and the choices are allowed.
It creates the repository, pipeline, namespace and a small database with default settings.
The service is added to the catalog with its owner, tier and links to dashboards.
The portal shows the new repository link, the first deploy status and where to find help.

title: Turning a queue into a roadmap
summary: Requests are counted, ranked and answered with one thin slice.

steps.n: Teams send requests by chat and tickets, each worded in its own way.
The product manager tags each request with a type and counts how many teams and hours it affects.
Two request types account for most of the hours, so they move to the top of the roadmap.
Engineers automate the most common case first and leave rare variations for later.
Release notes go to the teams with a short survey asking whether the slice removed the pain.
Requests of that type fall and adoption of the new workflow shows in the metrics.

title: A team stays on the path
summary: A service is created on the path and later receives an update automatically.

steps.n: The team chooses the web service path and sets a name and owner.
The template writes code, a pipeline, a health endpoint and default alerts into a new repository.
The pipeline builds, scans and deploys the service so the first release works the same day.
Months later the platform team releases a template version with a runtime security fix.
The bot opens a pull request in every repository that uses the path with the change applied.
The team reads a short summary, runs its tests and merges, so it gets the fix without manual work.

title: Tracing one deploy across the planes
summary: A single deploy crosses the control, delivery, resource and security planes.

steps.n: The developer asks the portal to deploy version 1.4 of the service to staging.
The portal calls the delivery system with the service name, version and target environment.
The delivery system asks the security plane whether the image passes the scan and policy rules.
Security approves, and the decision with its evidence is stored for audit.
Delivery applies the new version to the cluster resources defined for staging.
Health and rollout status flow back to the portal so the developer sees the result in one place.

title: Keeping the catalog true
summary: Descriptors in code are validated and checked against the team directory each night.

steps.n: The owner changes the owner field in the descriptor file in the same pull request as the code.
The catalog reads the descriptor on merge and updates the service page.
Each night the catalog asks the directory whether every listed owner team still exists.
The directory reports one team that was disbanded and no longer exists.
The catalog opens a ticket for the stale entry and assigns it to the service lead.
Alert routing reads the owner from the catalog, so fixing the entry sends pages to the right team.

title: A self-service workflow with checks
summary: Validate, create, retry and report, so a request never half completes in silence.

steps.n: The requester fills in a short form and submits it.
The workflow asks policy whether the name, owner and region are allowed before it creates anything.
It creates the repository with a key that makes the step safe to repeat.
It registers the service and the catalog answers with a temporary error.
The workflow waits and retries the registration, which succeeds on the second try.
The requester receives links to the repository and the catalog entry, with a record of each step.

title: From a Database object to a cloud instance
summary: A small custom resource is turned into real resources and reports honest status.

steps.n: The developer applies a small Database object with a size and a name.
The controller watches for Database objects and finds the new one.
It picks the composition that adds encryption, backups, tags and a network rule.
It calls the cloud API to create the instance and related resources.
The cloud reports that the instance is being created and later that it is available.
The controller sets conditions and writes the connection details into a secret for the application.

title: A policy through audit, warn and enforce
summary: A new rule moves through stages so teams can fix problems before anything is blocked.

steps.n: The platform team writes a rule that requires a resource limit on every container.
The rule runs in audit mode and records which workloads would have failed.
The team sends each owner a list of their workloads with a one line fix.
The pipeline begins to show a warning with the fix when a change breaks the rule.
Owners add limits and the audit count falls toward zero.
The rule is enforced for new and changed workloads, with a time-limited exception route.

title: Creating a tenant and a preview
summary: A namespace is created with quotas, policy and a time to live.

steps.n: A team asks for a namespace for a new service.
The workflow creates it with labels for owner, environment and cost centre.
It adds role bindings, a resource quota, a default network policy and a pod security level.
A pull request opens a short-lived preview namespace that carries an expiry label.
Each night the sweeper lists previews and finds those past their expiry.
Expired namespaces are deleted and the count is reported, so a failed event cannot leave them behind.

title: From a bill to a team report
summary: Labels and a sharing rule turn raw cost into a number each owner can act on.

steps.n: The monthly cost data is exported with the labels attached to each resource.
A policy has required owner and environment labels on new resources, so most lines have an owner.
Shared cluster cost is split by each team requested share of CPU and memory.
Capacity nobody requested is shown as its own line instead of being hidden in the shares.
Each owner receives a report with spend, trend and cost per unit of product value.
Owners remove waste and finance sees the unallocated amount shrink month by month.

title: Reading signals together
summary: Delivery numbers, a survey and onboarding time are read as one picture.

steps.n: Deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore are taken from the pipeline.
A short quarterly survey asks about blockers, tooling and how easy it is to ship.
The platform records the time it takes a new engineer to make a first production change.
The review sets the three views side by side without ranking teams.
The team and platform look for friction, such as a slow pipeline mentioned in the survey.
They agree one change, set a target and plan to read the same signals next quarter.

title: Moving services in waves
summary: A migration runs from pilot to removal of the old system.

steps.n: Two teams that want the new path migrate first and give feedback on the kit.
The platform shares an inventory script, automation and a checklist of checks.
Teams migrate in dated waves and each wave reports what blocked it.
The old system gets a published end date and owners for any remaining exceptions.
After the date the old pipelines and servers are removed and their credentials are revoked.
Security confirms no service still depends on the old system and closes the migration.

title: Failure and recovery: a repository with no owner
summary: A workflow fails halfway and the fix makes it safe to repeat.

steps.n: A team requests a new service through the workflow.
The workflow creates the repository and pipeline successfully.
Registration returns an error and the workflow stops without retrying.
The requester sees a generic failure and assumes nothing was created.
The team pushes code to the repository anyway, so it runs for two weeks with no owner in the catalog.
A new nightly job lists repositories without catalog entries and finds this one.
The workflow is changed to retry with backoff and to resume from the failed step with a safe key.
Failures now go to the requester with the failed step and a link to retry, and the sweeper stays as a backstop.

title: Failure and recovery: a policy that blocked a rollback
summary: A rule applied to old workloads delayed an incident fix.

steps.n: A release breaks the checkout service and the engineer decides to roll back.
The engineer sends a rollback to the previous version of the deployment.
The new rule requires a cost centre label and the old version does not have one, so it is denied.
The engineer pages the platform team while the outage continues.
The platform team grants an audited, time-limited exception and the rollback proceeds, fifteen minutes late.
The policy is changed to apply only to resources created after a set date.
The pipeline now tests the policy against previous versions and a rollback before any policy ships.
A short guide explains the exception route, who approves and how it is recorded.
